title: Same ADC idea, wrong order of operations. value = 1000. What does this print?
explain: value / 1023 is integer division: 1000 / 1023 = 0. Then 0 * 5000 = 0. Multiply first, then divide: value * 5000L / 1023 = 4887. Rule: in fixed-point math, keep the divide as the last step.

title: Your first LED circuit, but on a 3.3 V pin. Red LED drops about 2 V, resistor is 330 Ω. What is the current?
explain: The resistor sees 3.3 V - 2 V = 1.3 V. I = U / R = 1.3 / 330 = 3.9 mA. The LED is dimmer than on 5 V (9 mA with 330 Ω). The LED voltage drop does not change much, so a lower supply gives much less current.

title: A deadline set just before the wrap. now = 5, deadline = 0xFFFFFFF0. What does this print (naive, then signed difference)?
explain: Naive now >= deadline is 0: 5 is smaller than 0xFFFFFFF0, but the deadline is already passed in real time. now - deadline wraps to 21. Cast to int32_t gives +21, so >= 0 is true (1). The signed difference works when the times are less than about 24 days apart.

title: Ring buffer, size 4, power of two. Full when next(head) == tail. 6 bytes arrive and nobody reads. How many are stored?
explain: The buffer keeps one slot empty. Otherwise head == tail would mean both empty and full. So size N stores N - 1 bytes. The mask (head + 1) & (N - 1) wraps the index without a division. Only the ISR writes head and only loop() writes tail, so no lock is needed.

title: Uno. You add the Servo library and attach a servo on pin 5. Which pins lose analogWrite() now?
explain: The Servo library takes Timer1 on the Uno to make its pulses. Pins 9 and 10 get their PWM from Timer1, so analogWrite() stops working there, even if no servo is on them. The servo pin itself can be any pin. Plan your PWM LEDs on 3, 5, 6 or 11.

title: Button with an external 10 kΩ pull-up to 5 V. The button is pressed and connects the pin to GND. What current flows through the resistor?
explain: The pin is at 0 V, so the resistor has 5 V across it. I = 5 / 10000 = 0.5 mA. This is small but it is wasted as long as the button is held. On a battery device use a bigger pull-up, for example 100 kΩ, or the internal pull-up.

title: The counter counts the first press only. Later presses do nothing. Tap the bug.
explain: last is updated only inside the if. After the first press last stays LOW. On release the code does not store HIGH, so last == HIGH is never true again. Update last on every loop run, after the check, outside the if.

title: Sometimes the LED on PA6 flips by itself, or the PA5 write is lost. Tap the risky line.
explain: ODR |= is read, modify, write. If TIM2 fires between the read and the write, main writes back the old PA6 value and the toggle is lost. The ISR itself is fine. In main use BSRR: GPIOA->BSRR = 1u << 5 to set and 1u << (5 + 16) to reset. One write, no race.

pr.title: Simplify the blink timer
pr.author: junior-dev
pr.body: The subtraction was hard to read. This version says what we mean.

explain: last_ms + 500 wraps near the end of the 32-bit range. Then millis() >= small number is true at once, and the LED blinks like crazy for a moment. Or it is false for 49 days. Keep the subtraction: unsigned math gives the right elapsed time over a wrap. Also read millis() once.

title: ISR to loop(): flag, counter or queue?
bullets: Flag (volatile bool): one event is enough. A second press before loop() runs is lost. Clear it in loop().
Counter (volatile uint8_t): count events. Reset with interrupts off, or you lose events (read, then zero is a race).
Ring buffer: every event with data (bytes, timestamps) matters. ISR writes head, loop() writes tail.
Wider than the CPU word (uint16_t/uint32_t on the Uno)? Copy it with interrupts off.
Always: short ISR, no Serial.print, no delay().
